label: Letter
summary: A heartfelt letter to someone in your life, built from real moments you've already told.

slots.label: Opening Moment
slots.description: A specific moment or image to open on — a callback to a shared memory, not an abstract feeling. What the letter opens with sets whether it reads as earned or generic.

slots.label: Who They Are
slots.description: Who this person is beyond their role in the author's life — the thing the author actually sees in them.

slots.label: Shared History
slots.description: The 2-4 specific anecdotes the letter is built from — real scenes, not summarized habits.

slots.label: What I See in Them
slots.description: What the author admires or notices that this person may not fully see in themselves.

slots.label: What I Want Them to Know
slots.description: The honest, earned thing the letter lands on — not a tidy bow, the thing that's actually true.

research.basis: The gratitude-letter literature (Seligman 2005) found its largest acute effects came from concrete, specific detail — what the person did and how it affected the author's life — not general sentiment, which is why this format opens on a scene rather than a feeling. McAdams' five-slot scene probe is the mechanism for the 2-4 anecdotes the template calls for. Slot order follows the escalating self-disclosure structure Aron et al. (1997) found does the actual work of closeness: who they are, then shared history, then admiration, before naming what needs to be said.
citations: Seligman, Steen, Park & Peterson 2005 — gratitude letter/visit produced the largest acute happiness gains of five tested positive-psychology exercises, driven by concrete specificity; gains attenuate by 6 months.
McAdams, Life Story Interview II — five-slot scene probe (what happened/where/who/felt/what it says about you) is the depth mechanism for anecdotes.
Aron et al. 1997 (PSPB) — escalating, reciprocal self-disclosure structure produces closeness; the structure itself does the work, not any single question's content.

ai_context: When source material supports it, name the concrete effect this person's action or presence had on the author's life — what they did, how it changed things — rather than general praise; this specific-effect naming is what the gratitude-letter research found carries the emotional charge.
